Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute poisoning from agricultural organophosphate/carbamate pesticides; high mortality via oral ingestion, inhalation, or dermal absorption.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) enzyme, causing acetylcholine accumulation at muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS synapses.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: DUMBBELSS (Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia, Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation, Sweating); fasciculations, paralysis, seizures, coma.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Red blood cell / serum cholinesterase activity (<20-50%); Atropine stat (1.8-3 mg IV double q3-5m until clear chest lungs/dry secretions) + Pralidoxime (oxime).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute toxic hepatopathy caused by intentional or accidental ingestion of >7.5-10 g (or >150 mg/kg) paracetamol.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Excess N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) toxic metabolite depletes hepatic glutathione, causing hepatocellular necrosis.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Phase 1: Nausea/vomiting. Phase 2 (24-48h): RUQ pain, elevated AST/ALT. Phase 3 (72-96h): Jaundice, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, AKI, liver failure.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Serum paracetamol level plotted on Rumack-Matthew nomogram; elevated AST/ALT/INR; N-acetylcysteine (NAC) IV/oral stat (most effective within 8 hours).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute toxicity from heroin, morphine, methadone, fentanyl, or codeine ingestion/injection.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Overstimulation of mu-opioid receptors in CNS depresses brainstem respiratory center and blunts responsiveness to hypercapnia/hypoxia.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Opioid triad: CNS depression/coma, pin-point pupils (miosis), and severe respiratory depression/apnea; hypothermia, bradycardia, pulmonary edema.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Clinical diagnosis; urine toxicology screen; ABG showing respiratory acidosis; immediate bag-valve-mask ventilation + IV/IM Naloxone (0.4-2 mg stat).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Envenomation by Russell's viper or Saw-scaled viper; primary toxicity is hemotoxic and vasculotoxic.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Procoagulant toxins activate clotting factors causing consumption coagulopathy (DIC-like state), microvascular damage, and local tissue necrosis.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Severe local swelling, blistering, active bleeding from bite site, gums, hematuria, hemoptysis, hypovolemic/septic shock, acute kidney injury.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: 20-Minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (20WBCT) showing uncoagulable blood; polyvalent Anti-Snake Venom (ASV) 10 vials IV in 0.9% NS over 1 hour.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Envenomation by Naja naja (Cobra) or Bungarus caeruleus (Krait); nocturnal bites frequently while sleeping.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Post-synaptic (Cobra) or pre-synaptic (Krait) neurotoxins block neuromuscular transmission at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Bilateral ptosis, diplopia, ophthalmoplegia, dysphagia, dysarthria, descending flaccid paralysis, respiratory muscle paralysis/apnea.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Neurological clinical signs; 20WBCT (usually normal); polyvalent ASV 10 vials IV + Neostigmine (0.5-2.5 mg IV) + Atropine (for post-synaptic neurotoxicity).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Life-threatening hyperthermic emergency defined by core body temperature >40°C (104°F) accompanied by severe CNS dysfunction.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Failure of thermoregulation leads to systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), cellular protein denaturation, multiorgan failure, and DIC.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Hyperpyrexia (>40°C), altered mental status, confusion, delirium, seizures, coma, hot dry skin (classic) or diaphoresis (exertional), hypotension.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Core (rectal) temperature >40°C; DIC panel, elevated CPK/renal function; immediate aggressive cooling (cold water immersion / evaporative mist + fan) to <38.5°C.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Severe, systemic, life-threatening Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction triggered by drugs (penicillins, NSAIDs), stings, or food.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Massive IgE-mediated degranulation of mast cells and basophils releases histamine, leukotrienes, and tryptase, causing systemic vasodilation and bronchospasm.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Urticaria, angioedema (lip/tongue/airway swelling), stridor, severe wheezing, profound hypotension, dizziness, collapse, abdominal cramps.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Clinical diagnosis; serum tryptase (retrospective); immediate Intramuscular Epinephrine / Adrenaline (1:1000, 0.5 mg IM anterolateral thigh stat, repeat q5-15m).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Severe ethanol ingestion coupled with chronic thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency common in alcohol use disorder.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Thiamine deficiency impairs pyruvate dehydrogenase, causing impaired cerebral glucose metabolism and oxidative neuronal damage in mammillary bodies.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Wernicke triad: Acute confusion/delirium, ataxia (broad-based gait), and ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus; hypoglycemia, stupor, hypothermia.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Bedside capillary blood glucose; clinical triad; High-dose IV Thiamine (500 mg IV TID x 3 days) ALWAYS administered BEFORE IV Dextrose infusion.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Thermal, chemical, or electrical injury involving deep partial-thickness or full-thickness destruction of skin surface area.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Massive systemic capillary leak driven by inflammatory cytokines leads to rapid fluid extravasation into interstitial space and burn shock.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Erythema, blistering, charred eschar, hypovolemic shock, oliguria, airway edema/stridor (inhalation injury), circumferential eschar constriction.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Percentage Total Body Surface Area (%TBSA) via Rule of Nines; Parkland Formula (4 mL x kg x %TBSA Ringer's Lactate in first 24h: 1/2 in first 8h).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Inhalation toxicity from incomplete combustion of carbonaceous fuels (generators, fires, faulty heaters) in enclosed spaces.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: CO binds hemoglobin with >200x affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin (COHb), shifting O2-Hb dissociation curve left and inhibiting cellular respiration.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Headache (most common early sign), dizziness, confusion, nausea, cherry-red skin (rare/late), angina, coma, seizures.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Arterial/venous blood gas co-oximetry showing elevated Carboxyhemoglobin (COHb >10-15%); 100% High-Flow Normobaric or Hyperbaric Oxygen (HBO).
